items.hint1: Think about what fills the large vacuole in a plant cell, and what that does to the cell when the vacuole is full.
items.hint2: A vacuole full of cell sap pushes the cytoplasm hard against the cell wall, and the cell becomes turgid. Protection is mainly the job of the cell wall, and sensitivity belongs to the whole organism, not to one part of a cell.
items.hint3: Two options are left, and they sound alike. One comes from thick, hardened cell walls in tissues such as sclerenchyma. The other comes from cells being swollen with water. Which of the two does the vacuole give?
items.solution:
Answer: C. support

The vacuole holds cell sap, a watery solution of sugars, salts and wastes, and that is its storage job. When it is full, it presses the cytoplasm against the cell wall and makes the cell firm, or turgid, and turgid cells packed together hold up the stems and leaves of non-woody plants.

How to tell: a plant that is short of water wilts. Its vacuoles lose water, the cells go soft, and the stem and leaves droop. Water the plant and the vacuoles fill again, the cells become turgid, and the plant stands up. That upright hold is support coming from the vacuole.

Why not the others:
A. protection: in a plant cell this is mainly the job of the cell wall and of outer layers such as the epidermis, not the vacuole.
B. strength: a turgid cell does feel firm, but in the syllabus strength comes from the cellulose cell wall and from strengthening tissues such as collenchyma and sclerenchyma.
D. sensitivity: this is the whole organism responding to its surroundings, and the vacuole has nothing to do with it.

Exam tip: when an option list offers both strength and support, link the vacuole and turgidity to support, and link the cell wall, collenchyma and sclerenchyma to strength.

items.hint1: Compare the salt concentration of solution III with the concentration inside the cell, then work out which way water will move.
items.hint2: Water moves by osmosis from a weaker salt solution to a stronger one. At 6%, solution III is stronger than the cell's 3%, so the cell loses water, and turgid describes a cell that has gained water.
items.hint3: Two of the remaining words describe a cell that has lost water, and one describes a cell that has burst. A plant cell has a cell wall and an animal cell does not. Which water-loss word belongs to a cell with a wall?
items.solution:
Answer: D. plasmolyzed

Water moves by osmosis across the cell membrane from a weaker solution into a stronger one. A plant cell placed in a solution stronger than its own contents loses water, its vacuole shrinks, and the living contents pull away from the cell wall. This is plasmolysis.

How to tell: the cells are about as strong as a 3% salt solution. Solution III is 6% salt, which is stronger, so it is hypertonic to the cell and water leaves the cell by osmosis. The firm cell wall keeps its shape while the membrane and cytoplasm shrink away from it, which is plasmolysis.

Why not the others:
A. turgid: a plant cell becomes turgid when it takes in water from a weaker solution, such as solution I at 1%.
B. crenated: this is the same loss of water in an animal cell such as a red blood cell, which has no cell wall, so the whole cell shrinks and wrinkles.
C. haemolysed: this is a red blood cell bursting after taking in too much water from a weaker solution, and a plant cell cannot burst because its wall holds it in.

Exam tip: in osmosis questions, compare the solution with the cell first to find which way water moves, then check the cell type. A plant cell becomes turgid or plasmolysed; an animal cell bursts or becomes crenated.

items.hint1: Name each labelled organ first from its size, shape and position. Then recall which juices act on fat in the small intestine, and where each juice is made.
items.hint2: Fat is handled in two steps: bile breaks it into tiny droplets, then the enzyme lipase splits the droplets into fatty acids and glycerol. Find the organ in the diagram that makes bile and the organ that makes lipase.
items.hint3: It comes down to two parts that are easy to include by mistake: the small sac labelled IV and the stomach labelled I. For each, ask whether it actually makes a substance that works on fat, or only stores one, or makes juices for other foods.
items.solution:
Answer: C. II and III

Fat is digested in two steps in the small intestine. Bile breaks large fat drops into tiny droplets, and the enzyme lipase then splits the droplets into fatty acids and glycerol, so the parts that secrete substances for fat digestion are the organ that makes bile and the organ that makes lipase.

How to tell: in the diagram, I is the bag at the top right where the gullet enters, the stomach. II is the long, thin organ lying just below the stomach, the pancreas. III is the large organ filling the upper left, the liver. IV is the small sac attached to the liver, the gall bladder. The pancreas (II) secretes pancreatic juice, which contains lipase, and the liver (III) secretes bile. That gives II and III.

Why not the others:
A. I, II and III: I is the stomach, whose juice in the syllabus carries pepsin and rennin for protein, plus hydrochloric acid, and none of these digests fat.
B. I and III: it adds the stomach, which does not belong, and it leaves out the pancreas, the main source of lipase.
D. I, III and IV: IV is the gall bladder, which only stores bile made by the liver and releases it into the duodenum, so it does not make or secrete bile. This option also adds the stomach and leaves out the pancreas.

Exam tip: when a question asks which organ secretes a substance, choose the organ that makes it, not the one that stores it. The liver makes bile; the gall bladder only stores it.

items.hint1: Recall what villi look like and where in the gut they are found, then ask what that shape is good for.
items.hint2: Villi give the ileum a huge surface area, and each one carries tiny blood vessels and a lacteal that carry digested food away. In the syllabus, water is taken up mainly in the colon, which has no villi.
items.hint3: Two options mention absorbing nutrients. The difference is whether digestion would fail too. Think about where pancreatic juice and bile do their work, and whether they need villi to do it.
items.solution:
Answer: C. absorption of nutrients only

Villi are tiny finger-like folds on the inner wall of the small intestine (ileum), and they are built for absorption. They give a very large surface area, their lining is only one cell thick, and each one carries blood capillaries and a lacteal that take digested food away.

How to tell: without villi the surface area of the ileum drops sharply, so much less digested food can pass into the blood and lymph. Digestion itself would carry on, because pancreatic juice and bile work on food in the space inside the gut, and intestinal juice comes from glands in the gut wall. Only the uptake of nutrients suffers.

Why not the others:
A. digestion of food only: the juices that digest food would still work without villi, and this option leaves out absorption, which is the real problem.
B. absorption of water: the syllabus gives this job mainly to the colon, which has no villi, so water uptake is not what villi are known for.
D. digestion of food and absorption of nutrients: this is the trap, but digestion by pancreatic juice, bile and intestinal juice goes on without villi, so only absorption is affected.

Exam tip: link each part of the gut to its main job: villi to absorption, enzymes and bile to digestion, the colon to water. Then read the options for small words such as 'only' and 'and', because they often decide between two answers that look alike.

items.hint1: Picture two very different habitats, a pond and a forest, and ask which conditions act in both of them.
items.hint2: Temperature and light both vary in water as well as on land, so both of them affect every habitat.
items.hint3: Two factors are left. For each one, ask what it actually measures, and whether that still makes sense at the bottom of a pond as well as in a forest.
items.solution:
Answer: B. humidity

Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air. It only has meaning where there is air, so it is a factor of land (terrestrial) habitats and not of water (aquatic) habitats, where organisms are already surrounded by water.

How to tell: test each factor in a pond and in a forest. Temperature changes in both. Light changes in both, and in water it fades with depth. Pressure acts in both: air pressure on land, and water pressure that rises the deeper you go. Humidity is the only one that needs air, so it is the exception.

Why not the others:
A. temperature: it affects life on land and in water alike, and a pond warms by day and cools at night just as the land does.
C. light: plants on land and algae in water both depend on it, and its strength changes with shade on land and with depth in water.
D. pressure: it is often taught as a water factor because it rises with depth, but air pressure also acts on land organisms and is listed among the climatic factors of land habitats.

Exam tip: for questions on which factor does not affect all habitats, test each option in both a pond and a forest. A factor that describes the air, such as humidity, belongs to land habitats; one that describes the water, such as salinity or turbidity, belongs to water habitats.

items.hint1: Picture the S-shaped growth curve of a population, and find the stage where numbers reach the most the habitat can support.
items.hint2: Carrying capacity is the largest number of fish the pond's food, space and oxygen can support. Once it is reached, the population cannot keep climbing, and it has no reason to keep falling while the pond stays the same.
items.hint3: Two options are left: one describes numbers that keep going up and down, the other numbers that hold level. Which matches the top of the S-shaped curve?
items.solution:
Answer: B. remains unchanged

Carrying capacity is the largest population a habitat can support with the food, space and oxygen it has. When a population reaches it, the birth rate equals the death rate, so the population stops growing and holds steady at that level. A real pond may show small ups and downs over the weeks, but they cancel out and the population stays the same.

How to tell: picture the S-shaped (sigmoid) growth curve. It starts slowly (lag phase), climbs steeply (exponential phase), then levels off into a flat top (stationary phase). Carrying capacity is the height of that flat top, and a flat line means the population is not changing.

Why not the others:
A. alternately increases and decreases: this is the tempting one, since a real population wobbles a little around carrying capacity, but those wobbles balance out and the growth curve shows a flat line, so the population is taken as unchanged.
C. increases only: growth has stopped, because the pond has no spare food or space for more fish.
D. decreases only: a steady fall would mean the pond can no longer support that number, so the population would no longer be at its carrying capacity.

Exam tip: tie carrying capacity to the flat top of the S-shaped curve. At that stage births equal deaths, so the population stays constant.

items.hint1: Start with the meaning of conservation, and what kind of thing it is meant to protect.
items.hint2: Conservation means using natural resources carefully, protecting them and renewing them where possible, so they last. Soil, water, forests and wildlife are all plainly conserved this way, through good farming, reserves and forest laws.
items.hint3: Two options are left. One cannot be replaced once it is used up, and the other is what households throw away. Remember that being impossible to replace is not the same as being impossible to conserve.
items.solution:
Answer: D. domestic wastes

Conservation is the careful use, protection and renewal of natural resources so that they last for people now and in the future. Only a natural resource can be conserved, and domestic wastes are not one: they are what is left over after use, and they are managed by safe disposal, reducing and recycling.

How to tell: ask of each option whether it is a natural resource we want to keep for the future. Minerals, soil, water, forests and wildlife all are, and the syllabus lists each of them for conservation. Household waste is something we want to get rid of safely, not keep.

Why not the others:
A. mineral resources: this draws students because minerals cannot be replaced once used up, but non-renewable does not mean they cannot be conserved, and they are made to last by using less and recycling metals.
B. soil and water: soil is conserved by crop rotation, cover crops, terracing and contour ploughing, and water by protecting its sources from pollution and waste.
C. forest and wildlife: these are conserved through forest reserves, game reserves and national parks, and through laws against over-hunting.

Exam tip: 'cannot be conserved' usually points to something that is not a natural resource at all. Do not confuse non-renewable, which means it cannot be replaced, with cannot be conserved.
